# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are two popular communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. This comparison is beneficial for teams looking to switch from a proprietary platform to a self-hosted, open-source solution, with the core use case being team collaboration and communication. The key reason someone would switch is to gain control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free and self-hosted, while Slack has a per-user monthly fee.
* Data ownership: Element allows teams to have full control over their data, whereas Slack stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Element requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, while Slack is generally easier to get started with.
* Scalability: Element can be more scalable than Slack, especially for large teams, since it can be self-hosted on the team's own servers.
* Feature difference: Element has end-to-end encryption for all conversations, while Slack only offers this feature for certain plans.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Pros:
  + Easy to set up and use
  + Wide range of integrations with other tools
  + Good mobile app support
  + Large user community
  + Regular updates with new features
* Cons:
  + Can be expensive for large teams
  + Limited control over data
  + Limited customization options
  + Can be distracting with notifications and noise
  + Limited end-to-end encryption
### Element
* Pros:
  + Free and self-hosted
  + Full control over data
  + End-to-end encryption for all conversations
  + Highly customizable
  + Can be more scalable than Slack
* Cons:
  + Requires technical expertise to set up and maintain
  + Limited mobile app support
  + Smaller user community
  + Not as many integrations with other tools
  + Can be complex to use for non-technical users

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and have a small to medium size, or for teams that are already invested in the Slack ecosystem. It's also a good choice for teams that don't require full control over their data and are willing to pay a premium for a hassle-free experience.
Element is a good choice for teams that require full control over their data, are looking for a self-hosted solution, and have the technical expertise to set it up and maintain it. It's also a good choice for large teams that want to reduce costs and have a high level of customization.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up an Element server and configure it to your needs.
3. Import your Slack data into Element using the Element import tool.
4. Configure any necessary integrations and settings in Element.
5. Test your Element setup to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Element is a promising platform, but it may not be production-ready for most users right now due to its complexity and limited mobile app support. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that Element requires a significant amount of technical expertise to set up and maintain, which can be a barrier for non-technical teams. However, for teams that value control over their data and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining a self-hosted solution, Element is a clear winner, and we recommend switching from Slack to Element.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't require many integrations and want a free, self-hosted solution.
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) that are looking to reduce costs and have the technical expertise to set up and maintain an Element server.
* Large teams (more than 50 users) that require full control over their data and are looking for a scalable, self-hosted solution.
* Teams that don't require mobile app support and are willing to use the web interface.
* Teams that don't require a wide range of integrations with other tools.

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is free and self-hosted, which means you can use it without paying any monthly fees.
### Is Element as easy to use as Slack?
No, Element requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, and its user interface can be more complex than Slack's.
### Can I integrate Element with other tools?
Yes, Element has a range of integrations with other tools, but not as many as Slack.
### Is my data secure with Element?
Yes, Element offers end-to-end encryption for all conversations, which means your data is secure and private.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Element?
Yes, you can export your Slack data and import it into Element using the Element import tool.

title: Notion vs Obsidian
comparison_markdown:
# Notion vs Obsidian

## Overview

All-in-one workspace combining notes, databases, wikis, and project management. is a popular proprietary tool in the productivity space. Obsidian is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Notion costs $8-$20/user/month; Obsidian is Free (local use)
- **License**: Notion is Proprietary; Obsidian is Proprietary (free personal)
- **Data ownership**: Obsidian can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Obsidian eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Obsidian has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Notion | Obsidian |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $8-$20/user/month | Free (local use) |
| License | Proprietary | Proprietary (free personal) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$400/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,600/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Notion

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Obsidian

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Notion if:** Notion is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Obsidian if:** Obsidian is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Notion in its standard export format, review Obsidian import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Obsidian is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Notion tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Obsidian instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Notion, switching to self-hosted Obsidian will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Notion until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Notion paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Obsidian free to use?
Yes. Obsidian is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Notion to Obsidian?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Notion data, follow the Obsidian import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Obsidian get regular updates?
Yes. Obsidian has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Obsidian without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Obsidian development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced August 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Notion](https://notion.so) and [Obsidian](https://obsidian.md) before making decisions.*

4. Configure Logseq to match your Notion setup, including setting up users and permissions.
5. Test your Logseq setup to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Logseq is not yet production-ready for most users due to its technical requirements and limited user support. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that Logseq requires a significant amount of technical expertise to set up and manage, which can be a barrier for non-technical teams. However, for teams who require full control over their data and are willing to invest time in setting up Logseq, it's a great choice. We recommend switching to Logseq if you're a large team or enterprise with technical expertise, but not if you're a small team or individual who values ease of use over data control.

## Who Should Switch

* Individuals who value data ownership and are comfortable with self-hosting
* Small teams of less than 10 users who are tech-savvy and don't need Notion's features

## FAQ

# GitHub vs GitLab (2026)

## Overview
GitHub and GitLab are two popular version control platforms used for managing and collaborating on software development projects. This comparison is beneficial for developers, teams, and organizations looking to choose between the two platforms or considering switching from one to the other. The core use case for both platforms is source code management, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data or reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: GitHub offers a free plan with limited features, while GitLab offers a free self-hosted option with more features.
* Data ownership: GitLab allows for self-hosting, giving users full control over their data, while GitHub stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: GitLab requires more technical expertise to set up, especially for self-hosting, while GitHub is generally easier to get started with.
* Scalability: Both platforms are scalable, but GitLab's self-hosted option allows for more flexibility in terms of customization and scalability.
* Feature difference: GitLab offers a built-in Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) tool, while GitHub relies on third-party integrations for CI/CD.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | GitHub | GitLab |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT (CE) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $350-$1050/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1400-$4200/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**GitHub:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Large community and ecosystem
* Integrates well with other GitHub tools
* Offers a free plan with limited features
* Limited control over data and customization options
**GitLab:**
* Offers a free self-hosted option with more features
* Gives users full control over their data
* Highly customizable and scalable
* Offers a built-in CI/CD tool
* Can be complex to set up and manage, especially for self-hosting

## When to Choose Each
GitHub is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams or individuals who want a simple and easy-to-use version control platform with a large community and ecosystem. It's also a good choice for teams that don't require a high level of customization or control over their data. GitLab, on the other hand, is a good choice for larger teams or organizations that require more control over their data and customization options. It's also a good choice for teams that want a self-hosted option and are willing to invest time and resources into setting it up and managing it.

## Migration Path
1. Export your GitHub repository using the GitHub export tool, which exports data in a JSON format.
2. Create a new repository on GitLab and import the exported data using the GitLab import tool.
3. Update any existing links or references to the old GitHub repository.
4. Test and verify that the migration was successful.
5. Update any integrations or tools that rely on the old GitHub repository.

## Our Take
GitLab is a production-ready platform for most users, offering a wide range of features and customization options. However, one specific technical limitation worth knowing is that GitLab's self-hosted option requires a significant amount of technical expertise to set up and manage. For teams that require a high level of customization and control over their data, GitLab is a good choice, but for smaller teams or individuals who want a simple and easy-to-use platform, GitHub may still be a better option.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams that require more control over their data and customization options
* Teams that want a self-hosted option and are willing to invest time and resources into setting it up and managing it
* Teams that require a built-in CI/CD tool
* Teams that are currently using GitHub's free plan and are looking for more features
* Teams with 10 or more users that want to reduce costs

## FAQ
### Is GitLab free?
GitLab offers a free self-hosted option, as well as a free plan with limited features on its cloud platform.
### Can I self-host GitHub?
No, GitHub does not offer a self-hosting option.
### Is GitLab easy to use?
GitLab can be complex to set up and manage, especially for self-hosting, but it offers a wide range of features and customization options.
### Can I migrate from GitHub to GitLab?
Yes, GitLab offers an import tool that allows you to migrate your GitHub repository to GitLab.
### Does GitLab offer a built-in CI/CD tool?
Yes, GitLab offers a built-in CI/CD tool, which is a key feature difference between GitLab and GitHub.

title: GitHub vs Gitea
comparison_markdown:
# GitHub vs Gitea

## Overview

The world largest code hosting and collaboration platform. Owned by Microsoft since 2018. is a popular proprietary tool in the developer-tools space. Gitea is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: GitHub costs Free / $7-$21/user; Gitea is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: GitHub is Proprietary; Gitea is MIT
- **Data ownership**: Gitea can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Gitea eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Gitea has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | GitHub | Gitea |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### GitHub

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Gitea

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [go-gitea/gitea](https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea) * ~44k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose GitHub if:** GitHub is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Gitea if:** Gitea is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from GitHub in its standard export format, review Gitea import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Gitea is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid GitHub tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Gitea instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for GitHub, switching to self-hosted Gitea will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on GitHub until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated GitHub paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Gitea free to use?
Yes. Gitea is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from GitHub to Gitea?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your GitHub data, follow the Gitea import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Gitea get regular updates?
Yes. Gitea has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Gitea without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Gitea development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced August 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [GitHub](https://github.com) and [Gitea](https://gitea.io) before making decisions.*
